title: An Cnoc Ruadh's salt-traders walk to An Cruinneachadh Mòr
summary: Word goes out along every road that Cruinneachadh an Àtha in the three thousandth year since the grove will be kept greater than any before it. Households of An Cnoc Ruadh's lake shore, among them An Cnoc Ruadh girl and her mother, walk the fourteen miles down with their salt wrapped against the damp.

title: The three grounds of the ford run together
summary: More households come in than the ford's three grounds, downstream, upstream and the rise beyond the river, were ever laid out to hold, until by the second morning no one can any longer say which bank belongs to whom, and a child sent for water is an hour finding her way back.

title: Amber, pots and flint change hands at the ford
summary: Potters of the north-west, a stranger from the far west with strings of drilled amber, and carriers of eastern flint trade the first day of An Cruinneachadh Mòr through, while households from opposite ends of the crowd sit down together to weigh what a marriage between their children might be worth.

title: The reciters mark the three thousandth year since the grove
summary: An old reciter of the hill tells those at his fire that the year is the three thousandth since the grove was lit, and that word of the count has been carried out along every road that summer, drawing to the ford households who had never before troubled to send anyone to an ordinary gathering.

title: The crowd opens for the king unbidden
summary: On the second morning the king comes down the hill road dressed as any herdsman, and the whole crowd between the road and the river opens a way for him without a word called, old people stepping back from the path with their eyes down as from nothing else at the gathering.

title: An Cnoc Ruadh's new holder is still called by his father's name
summary: Among the five who wade out to put their hands between the king's, An Cnoc Ruadh's own holder is so newly come to his hall that half the crowd on the bank still names him for his father before catching themselves.

title: Somhairle stands nearest the king in the rings
summary: Somhairle takes his place at the king's left hand in the river as the rings of the king's blood go in, two thousand nine hundred and sixty-two years old that summer and looking, those at the ford say afterward, every year of it.

title: Murchadh is pointed out among the king's blood
summary: Murchadh, who holds the northern plain for his father and has by then eleven sons of his own scattered among the rings, is pointed out by name on the bank, a head taller than most beside him and looking, past his twelve hundredth year, no older than a young man.

title: Eithne stands young-faced in the outer ring
summary: Eithne, not yet three hundred years old and looking a girl of twenty, stands laughing among the outer rings of the king's blood, named to the girl of An Cnoc Ruadh by a woman of the ford who knows the lines by heart.

title: The reciters reckon four hundred of the king's blood
summary: The naming of the king's children and their children runs from midday to sundown and is not finished when the light fails; word passes along the bank that the reciters have counted some four hundred of his blood standing in the river that day, more than at any gathering before it.

title: A boy of the west asks whether it is one family
summary: A boy of a western household, standing beside An Cnoc Ruadh girl at the bank while the naming goes on, asks her whether all of that in the water is truly one family, and neither child can find a plainer answer to give the other.

title: The east's absence is remarked and let go
summary: Women of An Cnoc Ruadh note at the fire that no household from east of the vein has come to the gathering a second year running, turn the matter over a little while without an answer, and let it go with the fine weather, unremembered again within the hour.

title: An Cnoc Ruadh girl trails her hand in the warm ford
summary: When the gathering has gone back to its fires and the king stands alone a while in the emptied ford at dusk, An Cnoc Ruadh girl, nearest the water of anyone left on the bank, finds it warm as bath-water round his legs and sees it smoke downstream of him in the last light.
